title: Intervals
tagline: Sort by start, sweep with a single pointer — and you've solved merge, insert, overlap, and meeting-room problems.
intro:
Interval problems involve ranges — `[start, end]` pairs — and ask you to merge them, insert into them, count overlaps, or schedule them. They look varied, but almost all of them yield to one move: **sort the intervals (usually by start), then sweep through once**, comparing each interval to the one before. Sorting imposes the order that makes overlap detection a simple O(1) comparison instead of an O(n) search.

The one idea you must nail is the **overlap test**: two intervals `[a, b]` and `[c, d]` overlap exactly when `a <= d AND c <= b` — or, once sorted by start, when the next interval's start is ≤ the current interval's end. Get that comparison right and merge, insert, and non-overlapping problems all fall out.

This module covers the overlap rule, the sort-and-sweep template for merging, interval insertion, and the meeting-rooms (max concurrent) pattern that needs a slightly different sweep.
objectives: Write the overlap condition for two intervals correctly
Apply the sort-by-start, sweep-once template to merge intervals
Insert a new interval into a sorted, non-overlapping list
Count maximum concurrent intervals (meeting rooms II)
Choose between sorting by start vs by end for a given problem
State why these are O(n log n) (dominated by the sort)

signals: Input is a list of [start, end] ranges
"Minimum meeting rooms" / "maximum overlap" / "can attend all meetings"
antiSignals: Single contiguous range over an array → sliding window
Points, not ranges → sorting or two pointers without overlap logic
Ranges over a tiny fixed domain → maybe a boolean/diff array is simpler

sections.heading: The big idea in plain words
sections.body:
Intervals are calendar blocks, each with a start and an end. Line them up by start time and walk left to right, gluing together any block that begins before the previous one finishes. Sorting first is the whole trick - it turns 'do any of these overlap?' into one quick neighbour comparison.

Example: `[1, 3]`, `[2, 6]`, `[8, 10]`. Sorted by start, compare `[1, 3]` with `[2, 6]`: since 2 is not after 3, they overlap, so merge them into `[1, 6]`. Then `[8, 10]` starts after 6, so it stands on its own. The result is `[1, 6]` and `[8, 10]` - cleanly merged in a single pass.

sections.heading: The overlap rule
sections.body:
An interval is a pair `[start, end]`. The single fact everything depends on:

| Relationship | Condition (intervals [a,b] and [c,d]) |
| --- | --- |
| **Overlap** | `a <= d AND c <= b` |
| **Sorted by start, [c,d] after [a,b] overlaps** | `c <= b` |
| **Adjacent/touching** | `c == b + 1` (or `c == b` if inclusive) |
| **Disjoint** | `c > b` (next starts after current ends) |

Once you sort by start, you only ever compare the *next* interval's start to the *current* merged interval's end — the overlap test simplifies to `next.start <= current.end`.

callouts.text: Decide up front whether intervals are inclusive ([1,3] covers 3) or half-open ([1,3) excludes 3). It changes whether touching endpoints count as overlap — ask the interviewer if unspecified.

sections.heading: Sort by start or by end? (decision flow)
sections.body:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A["Interval problem"] --> B{"What are you doing?"}
  B -- "Merge / insert / combine ranges" --> C["Sort by START, sweep and extend end"]
  B -- "Max concurrent / min rooms" --> D["Split into start/end events, sweep a counter"]
  B -- "Max non-overlapping / min removals" --> E["Sort by END (greedy), keep earliest finishers"]
```

Merging keeps order and extends the current end (sort by start). Counting concurrency tracks how many are open at once (event sweep). Selecting the most non-overlapping is the greedy 'sort by end' problem from the greedy module.

sections.heading: Merge intervals — the core template
sections.body: Sort by start. Keep a `merged` list; for each interval, if it overlaps the last merged interval (its start ≤ last end), extend that interval's end to the max of the two; otherwise append it as a new block. One pass after the sort.

sections.heading: Insert interval
sections.body: Given a sorted, non-overlapping list and a new interval, you can do it in O(n) without re-sorting: copy all intervals that end before the new one starts (no overlap, on the left), then merge the new interval with every interval it overlaps (extending its bounds), then copy the rest (on the right). Three clean phases.

codeExamples.label: Insert interval into sorted list
codeExamples.code:
def insert(intervals, new):
    res, i, n = [], 0, len(intervals)
    # 1. left: ends before new starts
    while i < n and intervals[i][1] < new[0]:
        res.append(intervals[i]); i += 1
    # 2. merge overlaps with new
    while i < n and intervals[i][0] <= new[1]:
        new[0] = min(new[0], intervals[i][0])
        new[1] = max(new[1], intervals[i][1]); i += 1
    res.append(new)
    # 3. right: starts after new ends
    while i < n:
        res.append(intervals[i]); i += 1
    return res

sections.heading: Meeting rooms II — max concurrency
sections.body: 'Minimum meeting rooms' = the maximum number of intervals overlapping at any instant. Two clean approaches: (1) a **min-heap** of end times — for each meeting sorted by start, pop any room whose meeting has ended, then push this meeting's end; the heap's peak size is the answer. (2) the **event/sweep-line**: split each interval into a +1 at start and −1 at end, sort all events, and track the running sum's maximum.

codeExamples.label: Minimum meeting rooms (heap)
codeExamples.code:
import heapq

def min_rooms(intervals):
    intervals.sort(key=lambda x: x[0])   # by start
    heap = []                            # end times in use
    for s, e in intervals:
        if heap and heap[0] <= s:        # a room freed up
            heapq.heappop(heap)
        heapq.heappush(heap, e)
    return len(heap)                     # rooms needed at peak

callouts.text: In the sweep-line approach, process an END event before a START event when they share the same time, so a meeting ending exactly when another begins reuses the room (if endpoints are exclusive).

interviewTalking: State the plan immediately: "Interval problems are sort-then-sweep. I'll sort by start, then walk once, and two intervals overlap when the next start is ≤ the current end — when they do, I extend the end; otherwise I start a new block." For room-counting, switch framing: "This is max concurrency, so I'll use a min-heap of end times (or a sweep line of +1/−1 events) and report the peak." Always give O(n log n) dominated by the sort, and clarify inclusive vs exclusive endpoints.
commonMistakes: Writing the overlap condition wrong — it's `a <= d AND c <= b`
Forgetting to sort first (the sweep relies on order)
Using max(end) when extending a merge, not just the new interval's end
Mishandling touching endpoints (inclusive vs exclusive) for meeting rooms
Sorting by start when the greedy 'max non-overlapping' problem needs sort by end
Re-sorting on insert when a single O(n) three-phase pass suffices
complexityNotes: Merge, and most interval problems, are O(n log n) time (sort) + O(n) sweep, O(n) output space. Insert into an already-sorted list is O(n). Meeting rooms with a heap is O(n log n); the sweep-line is O(n log n) for sorting the events.
